hook: Leo Breiman earned a physics degree from Caltech in 1949, a master's degree in mathematics from Columbia in 1950, and a PhD from UC Berkeley in 1954, after which he taught probability theory at UCLA. He later resigned his tenured position to spend more than a decade as an independent statistical consultant, working on problems like traffic pattern and ozone level prediction, before joining the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980. With Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen and Charles Stone he co-developed Classification and Regression Trees, published in 1984, and in 1996 he introduced Bagging, a method of averaging predictions across bootstrap samples to reduce variance. In 2001 he introduced Random Forests, an ensemble of randomized decision trees that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms, and published Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, an influential essay on competing approaches to statistical inference. He died at his home in Berkeley, California, on July 5, 2005, following a prolonged illness.

quick_facts: Co-developed Classification and Regression Trees (CART) with Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen, and Charles Stone
Introduced Bagging (bootstrap aggregating) in 1996 to reduce prediction variance
Introduced the Random Forests algorithm in 2001, combining many decision trees into a single predictor
Began his career teaching probability theory at UCLA before leaving academia for over a decade to work as an independent statistical consultant
Joined the UC Berkeley Department of Statistics faculty in 1980 and remained active in research until his death in 2005

achievements.title: Classification and Regression Trees (CART)
achievements.impact: Co-developed a decision tree methodology for classification and regression, published as a book in 1984, that became a standard tool in statistics and machine learning.

achievements.title: Bagging predictors, 1996
achievements.impact: Introduced a method of averaging predictions from multiple bootstrap samples to reduce model variance.

achievements.title: Random Forests, 2001
achievements.impact: Developed an ensemble method combining many randomized decision trees, described in Machine Learning journal, that became one of the most widely used machine learning algorithms.

achievements.title: Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures, 2001
